questions.question: What is an ER diagram and what are its main components?
questions.title: ER Diagram — Entity Relationship Diagram Basics
questions.direct_answer: An ER (Entity-Relationship) diagram is a visual blueprint for a database schema. Main components: Entity (table), Attribute (column), Relationship (connection between entities), Cardinality (1:1, 1:N, M:N). ER diagrams are created before writing DDL.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands ER diagrams as a design tool and knows the core components used to model data structure
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not realizing that M:N relationships in the ER diagram cannot be directly implemented and require a junction table in the actual schema
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the translation from ER diagram to actual SQL DDL, specifically how a many-to-many relationship becomes a junction table with two foreign keys

sections.title: ER Diagrams as Database Blueprints
sections.content:
An **ER diagram** is the architectural sketch you draw before building a relational database. It's a visual language that captures **entities** (things you want to store, like Customer or Order), **attributes** (details about those things, like name or order_date), and **relationships** (how entities connect, like "Customer places Order").

Think of it like a floor plan for a house: you wouldn't start construction without knowing where the rooms connect. The diagram uses shapes—rectangles for entities, ovals for attributes, diamonds for relationships—to show structure at a glance. **Cardinality** labels (1:1, 1:N, M:N) define how many instances relate. ER diagrams are created in the design phase, translated into SQL DDL (Data Definition Language), then used to generate actual tables. Without this step, you risk creating a tangled schema full of redundancy and orphaned data.

sections.title: ER Diagram for a Blog Schema
ER Diagram Components in SQL
sections.content:
-- Entity: Customer (rectangle in ER diagram)
CREATE TABLE customer (
    customer_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,  -- Primary key attribute
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,          -- Simple attribute
    email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- Entity: Order (another rectangle)
CREATE TABLE "order" (
    order_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    order_date DATE NOT NULL,
    total_amount DECIMAL(10,2),
    customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL,         -- Foreign key (1:N relationship)
    CONSTRAINT fk_customer FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) 
        REFERENCES customer(customer_id)
);

-- Relationship: Customer "places" Order
-- Cardinality: 1:N (one customer, many orders)
-- Implementation: FK on the N side (order table)

sections.title: When to Create ER Diagrams
sections.content:
Use ER diagrams when **starting a new project** where the database schema is undefined—draw the ER diagram before writing a single CREATE TABLE statement.

Use them during **team design reviews** to communicate schema decisions visually; non-technical stakeholders can understand entities and relationships even if they can't read SQL.

Use them when **refactoring an existing schema**—reverse-engineer the current structure into an ER diagram to identify normalization problems, missing relationships, or redundant attributes. In Spring Boot projects, draw the ER diagram first, then map entities to JPA classes using the diagram as your guide.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Skipping ER diagrams entirely**: Freshers jump straight to coding JPA entities without designing the schema, leading to denormalized tables, missing foreign keys, and data integrity issues discovered too late.
- **Drawing M:N relationships without junction tables**: Beginners draw a many-to-many diamond and think it translates directly to SQL, not realizing the ER diagram is abstract and requires a bridge table in the actual schema.
- **Confusing attributes with entities**: Marking phone_number as an entity instead of an attribute of Customer, creating unnecessary tables and complexity when a simple VARCHAR column would suffice.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Entity**: A thing you store data about, shown as a rectangle, becomes a table in SQL
**Attribute**: A property of an entity, shown as an oval, becomes a column in that table
**Relationship**: A connection between entities, shown as a diamond, implemented with foreign keys
**Cardinality**: Defines how many instances relate (1:1, 1:N, M:N), determines FK placement
**Primary Key**: Underlined attribute in the ER diagram, becomes PRIMARY KEY constraint in SQL
**M:N relationships**: Cannot be directly implemented, require a junction table with two foreign keys
**ER-to-SQL translation**: The diagram is abstract, you manually translate it to DDL statements

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: An ER diagram is a visual blueprint for a database schema. It's what you draw before writing SQL. The main components are entities, which are the things you want to store—like Customer or Order—and they become tables. Attributes are properties of those entities—like name or email—and they become columns. Relationships show how entities connect, like Customer places Order, and you implement them with foreign keys. Cardinality defines how many instances relate: one-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many. For example, one customer can place many orders, that's a one-to-many relationship, so you'd put a customer_id foreign key in the order table. The tricky part for freshers is many-to-many relationships. In the ER diagram you just draw a diamond labeled M:N, but in the actual database you can't implement that directly. You need a junction table with foreign keys pointing to both sides. For instance, if students enroll in courses, you'd create an enrollments table with student_id and course_id. That's the translation from abstract diagram to concrete schema. The ER diagram keeps your design clean and helps you catch mistakes before you start coding.

questions.question: What is cardinality in database relationships?
questions.title: Cardinality in Database Design — 1:1, 1:N, M:N
questions.direct_answer: Cardinality defines how many instances of one entity relate to another. Types: 1:1 (one person has one passport), 1:N (one customer has many orders), M:N (many students can enroll in many courses). Cardinality determines how tables are related via foreign keys.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can identify relationship types and translate them into correct SQL foreign key design
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not understanding that M:N cardinality cannot be implemented with a single foreign key and requires a junction table
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Provide concrete real-world examples for each cardinality type and explain the SQL implementation details including where the foreign key goes

sections.title: Cardinality Defines Relationship Multiplicity
sections.content:
**Cardinality** is the numeric rule that governs how many instances of one entity can relate to another. It answers questions like "Can one customer place multiple orders?" or "Does an employee belong to one department or many?" The three fundamental types are **1:1** (one-to-one), **1:N** (one-to-many), and **M:N** (many-to-many).

Cardinality isn't just theoretical—it directly controls how you design your SQL schema. A 1:N relationship means the foreign key goes on the N side. A 1:1 relationship means you pick one side to hold the foreign key (usually the optional or dependent entity). An M:N relationship cannot be stored with a single foreign key at all; you must create a junction table. Think of cardinality as the "capacity" of a relationship: a parking spot (1:1) holds one car, a garage (1:N) holds many cars, a city parking system (M:N) connects many drivers to many spots over time.

sections.title: The Three Cardinalities in One ER Diagram
Implementing Each Cardinality Type
Choosing the Right Cardinality
sections.content:
Use **1:1** when two entities are tightly coupled but you want to separate them for performance or security—like User and CreditCard where sensitive data lives in a separate table with restricted access.

Use **1:N** when one entity owns or contains many instances of another—a Customer has many Orders, a Blog has many Posts, a Category contains many Products. This is the most common cardinality in real applications.

Use **M:N** when both sides can relate to multiple instances of the other—Students enroll in multiple Courses and each Course has multiple Students, or Authors write multiple Books and Books can have multiple Authors. The key signal for M:N is bidirectional plurality.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Placing FK on the wrong side in 1:N**: Freshers put a customer_id column in the customer table pointing to orders, which inverts the relationship and only allows one order per customer. The FK must go on the many side (order table).
- **Trying to implement M:N with a single FK**: Attempting to store multiple course IDs in a single column as a comma-separated string (student table with courses='101,203,305') breaks normalization, makes querying impossible, and violates foreign key constraints.
- **Using 1:1 when 1:N is correct**: Modeling Address as 1:1 with Customer when customers can have multiple addresses (shipping, billing)—forcing a redesign later when the business requirement surfaces.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **1:1 cardinality**: One entity instance relates to exactly one instance of another, FK goes on the dependent side with UNIQUE constraint
**1:N cardinality**: Most common type, FK always placed on the N (many) side, allows one parent to own multiple children
**M:N cardinality**: Cannot be directly implemented, requires a junction table with composite primary key of both foreign keys
**FK placement rule**: In 1:N, the foreign key column lives in the table on the many side, referencing the one side's primary key
**UNIQUE constraint**: Enforces 1:1 cardinality by preventing duplicate values in the foreign key column
**Junction table attributes**: Can store relationship-specific data like enrolled_date or quantity beyond just the two FKs
**Cardinality in JPA**: Mapped with at-OneToOne, at-ManyToOne, at-OneToMany, and at-ManyToMany annotations

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Cardinality defines how many instances of one entity can relate to another. There are three types. One-to-one means each instance on both sides relates to exactly one instance on the other side—like a person and their passport. You implement this by putting a foreign key on one side with a UNIQUE constraint. One-to-many is the most common—one customer can place many orders, one department has many employees. You implement this by placing the foreign key on the many side. So in the order table, you'd have a customer_id foreign key pointing to the customer table. Many-to-many is where it gets tricky. Many students can enroll in many courses and each course can have many students. You can't implement this with a single foreign key. You need a junction table—let's call it enrollment—with two foreign keys, student_id and course_id. The composite primary key would be both columns together. Freshers often try to store M:N as a comma-separated list in one column, but that breaks referential integrity and makes querying impossible. The key thing to remember is cardinality determines where the foreign key goes. For one-to-many, it always goes on the many side. For many-to-many, you always need that bridge table.

questions.question: What is a junction table and when do you use it?
questions.title: Junction Table (Bridge Table) in Database Design
questions.direct_answer: A junction table (bridge table) resolves a many-to-many relationship. It contains foreign keys referencing the primary keys of both related tables, plus any additional relationship attributes. Example: enrollments(student_id, course_id, enrolled_date) for Student-Course M:N.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of how to implement many-to-many relationships in relational databases
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking a many-to-many relationship can be stored with just a foreign key in one table or as a comma-separated list
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that the junction table can store relationship-specific attributes and show a real Spring Boot entity mapping with at-ManyToMany

sections.title: Junction Tables Resolve Many-to-Many Relationships
sections.content:
A **junction table** (also called a **bridge table**, **associative table**, or **join table**) is the solution to a problem that stumps beginners: how do you store a many-to-many relationship in a relational database? The answer is you can't—at least not directly. Relational databases only support one-to-many via foreign keys. A junction table transforms an M:N relationship into two 1:N relationships. It sits between the two entities and holds **foreign keys** to both, plus any **relationship-specific attributes** like enrolled_date, quantity, or status. For example, Students and Courses have an M:N relationship. You create an enrollments table with student_id and course_id as foreign keys and a composite primary key of both columns. Now one student can link to many enrollment rows (1:N) and one course can link to many enrollment rows (1:N), effectively creating the M:N relationship.

Without this table, you'd be forced to denormalize data or use fragile comma-separated lists.

sections.title: A Junction Table Splits M:N into Two 1:N Links
Junction Table with Relationship Attributes
sections.content:
-- Two entities with M:N relationship
CREATE TABLE author (
    author_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE book (
    book_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    title VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    isbn VARCHAR(13) UNIQUE
);

-- Junction table: author_book
CREATE TABLE author_book (
    author_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    book_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    contribution_role VARCHAR(50) DEFAULT 'author',  -- Relationship attribute
    royalty_percentage DECIMAL(5,2),                 -- Another relationship attribute
    PRIMARY KEY (author_id, book_id),                -- Composite PK prevents duplicates
    CONSTRAINT fk_author FOREIGN KEY (author_id) REFERENCES author(author_id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    CONSTRAINT fk_book FOREIGN KEY (book_id) REFERENCES book(book_id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);

-- Query: Find all books by an author
SELECT b.title, ab.contribution_role 
FROM book b
JOIN author_book ab ON b.book_id = ab.book_id
WHERE ab.author_id = 42;

sections.title: Wrong: M:N Faked with a Comma-Separated Column
sections.content:
```sql
-- Anti-pattern: cram many tag ids into one column
CREATE TABLE post (
    post_id   BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    title     VARCHAR(200),
    tag_ids   VARCHAR(255)   -- e.g. '12,45,9' — violates 1NF
);

-- Finding every post with tag 9 needs fragile string matching:
SELECT * FROM post WHERE tag_ids LIKE '%9%';  -- also matches 19, 90, 109...
```

This breaks first normal form, blocks foreign-key constraints, and makes correct filtering nearly impossible.

sections.title: Right: M:N Resolved with a Junction Table
sections.content:
```sql
-- Junction table holds one row per (post, tag) pair
CREATE TABLE post_tag (
    post_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    tag_id  BIGINT NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (post_id, tag_id),
    CONSTRAINT fk_post FOREIGN KEY (post_id) REFERENCES post(post_id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    CONSTRAINT fk_tag  FOREIGN KEY (tag_id)  REFERENCES tag(tag_id)  ON DELETE CASCADE
);

-- Finding every post with tag 9 is a clean, indexable join:
SELECT p.* FROM post p
JOIN post_tag pt ON p.post_id = pt.post_id
WHERE pt.tag_id = 9;
```

The composite primary key blocks duplicate pairs and foreign keys guarantee referential integrity.

sections.title: When to Create a Junction Table
sections.content:
Use a junction table when **both entities can relate to multiple instances of the other**—the hallmark of M:N cardinality. Students enroll in many Courses, and each Course has many Students: create enrollments(student_id, course_id). Products belong to many Categories and Categories contain many Products: create product_category(product_id, category_id). Users can like many Posts and Posts can be liked by many Users: create post_likes(user_id, post_id, liked_at).

Use it when you need to **store data about the relationship itself**, not just the connection—like order_items(order_id, product_id, quantity, price), where quantity and price are attributes of the relationship, not of Order or Product alone. In Spring Boot, JPA automatically creates junction tables when you use the at-ManyToMany annotation.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Storing M:N as comma-separated values**: Freshers create a course_ids column in the student table with values like '101,203,305', breaking first normal form, making foreign key constraints impossible, and requiring string parsing in queries.
- **Forgetting the composite primary key**: Creating a junction table without PRIMARY KEY (entity1_id, entity2_id) allows duplicate relationships (same student enrolled in the same course twice), corrupting data integrity.
- **Not using CASCADE delete**: When an author is deleted but author_book rows remain orphaned, queries return inconsistent results; ON DELETE CASCADE ensures referential integrity by cleaning up junction rows automatically.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Junction table structure**: Minimum two foreign key columns referencing the primary keys of the related entities
**Composite primary key**: PRIMARY KEY (fk1, fk2) prevents duplicate relationships and enforces uniqueness
**Relationship attributes**: Junction tables can store data about the relationship itself, like quantity or timestamp
**Cascading deletes**: Use ON DELETE CASCADE to automatically remove junction rows when parent entities are deleted
**at-ManyToMany in JPA**: Spring Data JPA generates junction tables automatically, but you lose control over relationship attributes
**Explicit junction entity**: For complex relationships with attributes, create a full JPA entity class for the junction table
**Querying M:N**: Always requires a JOIN through the junction table to traverse the relationship

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A junction table is how you implement a many-to-many relationship in a relational database. You can't store M:N directly because foreign keys only support one-to-many. So you create a bridge table that sits between the two entities. It contains foreign keys to both sides, turning one M:N into two 1:N relationships. For example, students and courses. A student can take many courses and a course has many students. You'd create an enrollments table with student_id and course_id as foreign keys. The primary key would be the combination of both columns—that's called a composite key—and it prevents a student from being enrolled in the same course twice. The cool thing about junction tables is you can also store attributes about the relationship itself. Like in enrollments, you might add an enrolled_date or a grade column. Those don't belong to the student or the course—they belong to the act of enrolling. In Spring Boot with JPA, you can use the at-ManyToMany annotation and Hibernate will create the junction table automatically. But if you need those relationship attributes, you should create an explicit entity class for the junction table, like an Enrollment class with at-ManyToOne relationships to both Student and Course. That gives you full control.

questions.question: What is the difference between total and partial participation in an ER diagram?
questions.title: Total vs Partial Participation
questions.direct_answer: Total participation means every entity in the set must participate in the relationship (double line in ER notation), while partial participation means some entities may not participate (single line).

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of participation constraints beyond basic entities and relationships, and their role in enforcing business rules
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing participation (mandatory vs optional relationship involvement) with cardinality (how many instances relate)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show how total participation translates to NOT NULL foreign key constraints and explain the business logic behind choosing total vs partial

sections.title: Participation Constraints Enforce Business Rules
sections.content:
**Participation** defines whether every instance of an entity **must** participate in a relationship or whether participation is optional. It's shown on the relationship line in ER diagrams: a **double line** indicates **total participation** (mandatory), a **single line** indicates **partial participation** (optional).

Total participation means 100% of entities on that side are involved. For example, if every Employee must be assigned to a Department, that's total participation from Employee—the line from Employee to the "works_in" relationship is doubled. Partial participation means some entities may not be involved. Not every Customer has placed an Order yet, so Customer has partial participation in the "places" relationship. This constraint translates directly to SQL: total participation becomes a **NOT NULL** foreign key, partial participation allows **NULL**. Think of participation as the business rule: "Is this relationship required or optional for this entity?"

sections.title: Total vs Partial Participation in an ER Diagram
Total vs Partial Participation in DDL
sections.content:
```sql
-- Total participation: every order MUST belong to a customer (NOT NULL FK)
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id          INT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id INT NOT NULL,                 -- total participation
    FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id)
);

-- Partial participation: a customer may exist with zero orders.
-- Nothing forces a customers row to appear in orders, so participation is optional.
```

Total participation is shown by a double line in the ER diagram and enforced with a NOT NULL foreign key.

rows: Double line from entity to relationship
Single line from entity to relationship
Nullable foreign key (FK can be NULL)
Every Employee works in a Department
Not every Customer has placed an Order

sections.title: Choosing Total vs Partial Participation
sections.content:
Use **total participation** when the relationship is a **business requirement**. Every Order must have a Customer (you can't have an anonymous order), so Order has total participation in the Order-Customer relationship—the customer_id foreign key in the order table is NOT NULL. Every Employee must belong to a Department (no floating employees), so employee.dept_id is NOT NULL.

Use **partial participation** when the relationship is **optional**. Not every Product is currently in an Order (new inventory), so Product has partial participation in Product-Order. Not every User has written a Comment, so User has partial participation in User-Comment. The participation constraint enforces referential integrity at the database level, preventing invalid states like an order without a customer.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing participation with cardinality**: Freshers think total participation means one-to-one or that partial participation means many-to-many—participation is about mandatory vs optional, cardinality is about how many instances relate (1:1, 1:N, M:N).
- **Not translating to NOT NULL**: Drawing total participation in the ER diagram but forgetting to add NOT NULL to the foreign key in SQL, allowing null values that violate the business rule.
- **Making everything total participation**: Defaulting all relationships to mandatory (NOT NULL) without checking business logic, forcing workarounds like dummy/placeholder entities just to satisfy the constraint when optional relationships are natural.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Total participation**: Every entity on that side must participate in the relationship, shown with double line in ER diagram
**Partial participation**: Some entities may not participate, relationship is optional, shown with single line
**SQL translation**: Total participation becomes NOT NULL foreign key, partial participation allows NULL
**Business rule enforcement**: Participation constraints encode mandatory vs optional relationships at the database level
**Not the same as cardinality**: Cardinality is about quantity (1:1, 1:N, M:N), participation is about requirement (must or may)
**Example (total)**: Every Order must have a Customer, so order dot customer_id NOT NULL
**Example (partial)**: Not every Customer has placed an Order yet, so Customer side is optional (single line)

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Participation defines whether an entity must be in a relationship or if it's optional. There are two types: total and partial. Total participation means every entity on that side has to participate. In ER diagrams you show it with a double line. For example, every order must have a customer—you can't have an anonymous order. So Order has total participation in the Order-Customer relationship. In SQL, that translates to a NOT NULL foreign key. The customer_id column in the order table can't be null. Partial participation means some entities might not be involved. Not every customer has placed an order yet—new customers haven't bought anything. So Customer has partial participation in the Order-Customer relationship. That's shown with a single line in the ER diagram, and in SQL the foreign key would be nullable. Freshers often confuse this with cardinality. Cardinality is about how many—one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many. Participation is about whether the relationship is required or optional. They're independent concepts. You can have a one-to-many relationship where the many side has total participation, meaning every child must have a parent. The key thing is participation constraints enforce business rules at the database level. If you model it as total participation, the database won't let you violate that rule.

How do you represent a mandatory one-to-one relationship in SQL?

groups.heading: Total
groups.text: Every row must join the relationship. A comment must belong to a post. In SQL that's a NOT NULL foreign key.

groups.heading: Partial
groups.text: Joining's optional. A user might never write a post. In SQL that's a nullable foreign key.

values: Foreign key set to NOT NULL.

items: Pick NOT NULL when the child makes no sense alone, like a comment that's lost without a post.
Allow NULL when the link's optional, like a user who hasn't set a profile photo.

beats.text: In our blog, a comment's post_id stays NOT NULL, so it's never an orphan. A profile photo can stay NULL. The gotcha: that rule comes straight from the diagram's participation lines.

speakable_v2.cap: Participation maps to one detail in SQL: NOT NULL or nullable. Small flag, big impact.

questions.question: What is a self-referencing (recursive) relationship in an ER diagram and how do you implement it?
questions.title: Self-Referencing Relationships
questions.direct_answer: A self-referencing relationship is when an entity has a relationship with itself, such as an Employee who manages other Employees; it is implemented with a nullable foreign key that references the same table.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of hierarchical data structures and how to model recursive relationships in relational databases
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not making the self-referencing foreign key nullable, which makes it impossible to store root nodes (employees with no manager, top-level categories)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention real-world use cases like organizational charts, category trees, and comment threads, and explain how to query hierarchical data with recursive CTEs

sections.title: Self-Referencing Relationships Model Hierarchies
sections.content:
A **self-referencing** or **recursive relationship** occurs when an entity has a relationship with itself—instances of the same entity are related to each other. The classic example is an **Employee** who manages other Employees: "Employee manages Employee" is a self-referencing 1:N relationship.

In the ER diagram, you draw a single entity with a relationship diamond looping back to itself, labeled with role names like "manager" and "subordinate" to distinguish the direction. Implementation is straightforward: add a **foreign key column** in the table that references the table's own primary key. For Employee, you'd have a manager_id column referencing employee_id. The critical detail: this foreign key **must be nullable** (allows NULL) to represent root nodes—the CEO has no manager, top-level categories have no parent. Self-referencing relationships model **hierarchies** like org charts, category trees, file systems, and threaded comments.

sections.title: A Self-Referencing Relationship Loops Back to the Same Table
sections.content:
```mermaid
erDiagram
    COMMENT ||--o{ COMMENT : "parent of"
    COMMENT {
        bigint comment_id PK
        bigint post_id FK
        bigint parent_comment_id FK "NULL for top-level"
        string body
    }
```

The COMMENT entity links to itself: one comment can be the parent of many replies. The loop is implemented by parent_comment_id, a foreign key into the same table. It must allow NULL so a top-level comment can exist with no parent.

sections.title: Self-Referencing Relationship Implementation
sections.content:
-- Employee manages Employee (organizational hierarchy)
CREATE TABLE employee (
    employee_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    title VARCHAR(50),
    manager_id BIGINT,                   -- Self-referencing FK (nullable)
    CONSTRAINT fk_manager FOREIGN KEY (manager_id) 
        REFERENCES employee(employee_id) ON DELETE SET NULL
);

-- Sample data: CEO (no manager) and two reports
INSERT INTO employee (name, title, manager_id) VALUES
    ('Alice CEO', 'Chief Executive Officer', NULL),  -- Root node
    ('Bob Manager', 'Engineering Manager', 1),
    ('Carol Dev', 'Software Developer', 2);

-- Query: Find all direct reports for a manager
SELECT e.name, e.title
FROM employee e
WHERE e.manager_id = 2;  -- Bob's reports

-- Recursive CTE: Get entire reporting chain
WITH RECURSIVE org_chart AS (
    SELECT employee_id, name, manager_id, 0 AS level
    FROM employee WHERE manager_id IS NULL  -- Start at root
    UNION ALL
    SELECT e.employee_id, e.name, e.manager_id, oc.level + 1
    FROM employee e
    JOIN org_chart oc ON e.manager_id = oc.employee_id
)
SELECT * FROM org_chart ORDER BY level, name;

sections.title: When to Use Self-Referencing Relationships
sections.content:
Use self-referencing relationships for **hierarchical data** where parent and child are the same type. Organizational charts (Employee manages Employee), category trees (Category contains subcategories), file systems (Folder contains folders), comment threads (Comment replies to Comment), task dependencies (Task depends on Task).

Use them when you need to represent **parent-child or part-whole relationships within a single entity type**. In Spring Boot with JPA, map self-referencing relationships using at-ManyToOne and at-OneToMany on the same entity class—Employee has at-ManyToOne manager and at-OneToMany subordinates. Query hierarchies using **recursive CTEs** in SQL (WITH RECURSIVE) or frameworks like Hibernate that support lazy-loading tree structures.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting to make FK nullable**: Freshers declare manager_id NOT NULL, making it impossible to insert the first employee (the CEO) because there's no one to reference as manager, causing a chicken-and-egg constraint violation.
- **Not handling circular references**: Allowing Employee A to manage Employee B while B manages A creates an infinite loop in traversal queries; application code must validate against cycles.
- **Ignoring deletion complexity**: Deleting an employee with subordinates without ON DELETE SET NULL or cascade logic leaves orphaned employees with invalid manager_id values, breaking referential integrity.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Self-referencing FK**: A foreign key column in a table that references the same table's primary key
**Nullable constraint**: FK must allow NULL to represent root nodes (CEO, top-level category, no parent)
**Hierarchical data**: Organizational charts, category trees, comment threads, file systems are classic use cases
**ER diagram notation**: One entity with a relationship diamond looping back to itself, labeled with role names
**Recursive CTE**: Use WITH RECURSIVE in SQL to query entire hierarchies in a single query, traversing parent-child links
**JPA mapping**: Use at-ManyToOne for parent reference and at-OneToMany for children collection in the same entity
**ON DELETE behavior**: Use SET NULL or CASCADE based on business logic for what happens when parent is deleted

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A self-referencing relationship is when an entity relates to itself. The most common example is an employee hierarchy. An employee has a manager, and that manager is also an employee. So it's a one-to-many relationship within the same entity—one manager has many subordinates, but they're all employees. You implement this with a foreign key that points to the same table. In the employee table, you'd have an employee_id as the primary key and a manager_id as a foreign key referencing employee_id. The critical thing is manager_id has to be nullable. Why? Because the CEO or the root of the hierarchy doesn't have a manager. If you make it NOT NULL, you can't insert that first record—you'd have a chicken-and-egg problem. Other real-world examples are category trees for e-commerce—a category can have subcategories, and those subcategories are also categories. Or comment threads on a blog post—a comment can be a reply to another comment. In Spring Boot, you'd have an Employee entity with a manager field annotated with at-ManyToOne pointing to Employee and a subordinates field with at-OneToMany also pointing to Employee. To query the entire hierarchy, you'd use a recursive CTE in SQL. That's a WITH RECURSIVE query that starts at the root and traverses down, collecting all descendants. Self-referencing relationships are how you model trees and hierarchies in relational databases.

What is a recursive CTE and how does it work?

Hierarchies have no fixed depth. You don't know how deep an org chart goes. One self-referencing key handles any depth without new tables.

questions.question: What is the difference between an attribute, a derived attribute, and a multi-valued attribute in an ER diagram?
questions.title: Attribute Types in ER Diagrams
questions.direct_answer: A simple attribute stores a single atomic value, a derived attribute is calculated from other attributes (shown with a dashed oval), and a multi-valued attribute can hold multiple values for one entity (shown with a double oval).

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of different attribute types in ER modeling and their impact on database schema design decisions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Storing multi-valued attributes as comma-separated strings in one column instead of normalizing them into a separate related table
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the translation of each attribute type to SQL—simple attribute to column, derived attribute to view or computed column, multi-valued attribute to 1:N relationship

sections.title: Attribute Types Shape Schema Design
sections.content:
Not all attributes are created equal. In ER modeling, attributes are classified by how they store and derive data. A **simple attribute** (or **atomic attribute**) holds a single indivisible value—name, email, age—and maps directly to a column in SQL. A **derived attribute** is calculated from other attributes rather than stored—age derived from birth_date, total_price from quantity times unit_price. In ER diagrams, derived attributes are shown with a **dashed oval** because they're not physically stored. A **multi-valued attribute** can hold multiple values for one entity—an Employee can have multiple phone_numbers or skills. It's shown with a **double oval**.

The key mistake freshers make: storing multi-valued attributes as comma-separated strings in a single column (skills='Java,Python,SQL'), which violates **first normal form** and breaks querying. The correct implementation is a **separate table** with a 1:N relationship: a skills table with employee_id as a foreign key, one row per skill.

sections.title: How Each Attribute Type Lands in the Schema
sections.content:
```mermaid
erDiagram
    USER ||--o{ USER_EMAIL : has
    USER {
        bigint user_id PK
        string username "simple"
        date birth_date "simple"
    }
    USER_EMAIL {
        bigint user_id FK
        string email "multi-valued split out"
    }
```

Simple attributes like username and birth_date stay as plain columns on USER. A multi-valued attribute (a user's many emails) moves into its own USER_EMAIL table with a foreign key back. A derived attribute such as age is not stored at all — it's computed from birth_date in a query or view.

sections.title: Translating Attribute Types to SQL
sections.content:
-- Simple attributes: direct columns
CREATE TABLE employee (
    employee_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,          -- Simple attribute
    birth_date DATE NOT NULL,            -- Simple attribute
    salary DECIMAL(10,2)                 -- Simple attribute
);

-- Derived attribute: not stored, computed in query or view
CREATE VIEW employee_summary AS
SELECT 
    employee_id,
    name,
    birth_date,
    EXTRACT(YEAR FROM AGE(birth_date)) AS age,  -- Derived: age from birth_date
    salary
FROM employee;

-- Multi-valued attribute: separate table with 1:N relationship
CREATE TABLE employee_skill (        -- Normalized multi-valued attribute
    employee_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    skill_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    proficiency_level VARCHAR(20),
    PRIMARY KEY (employee_id, skill_name),
    CONSTRAINT fk_employee FOREIGN KEY (employee_id) 
        REFERENCES employee(employee_id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);

-- Query: Find all skills for an employee
SELECT skill_name, proficiency_level
FROM employee_skill
WHERE employee_id = 42;

sections.title: When to Use Each Attribute Type
sections.content:
Use **simple attributes** for straightforward data that doesn't need calculation or repetition—first_name, email, status.

Use **derived attributes** when a value is always computed from existing data and you want to avoid storing redundant information—total_amount derived from sum of order items, age from birth_date, full_name concatenated from first_name and last_name. Store derived values only if computation is expensive and data changes rarely.

Use **multi-valued attributes** when an entity naturally has multiple instances of the same property—an Employee with multiple certifications, a Product with multiple images, a User with multiple email addresses. Always normalize multi-valued attributes into a separate table to maintain first normal form and enable efficient querying.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Storing multi-valued as CSV**: Freshers create a skills column with value 'Java,Python,SQL', breaking first normal form, making queries require string parsing (LIKE '%Java%'), and preventing proper indexing or foreign key constraints.
- **Storing derived attributes**: Physically storing age or total_price in the database when they can be calculated, leading to data inconsistency when birth_date or item prices change but the derived value isn't updated.
- **Not using computed columns**: In databases that support them (PostgreSQL GENERATED, MySQL VIRTUAL), freshers manually update derived values in application code instead of letting the database compute them automatically, increasing error risk.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Simple attribute**: Single atomic value, shown as regular oval, maps to a table column
**Derived attribute**: Calculated from other attributes, shown as dashed oval, not stored (computed in view or query)
**Multi-valued attribute**: Holds multiple values per entity, shown as double oval, requires separate table
**First normal form**: Multi-valued attributes violate 1NF if stored as CSV, must be normalized to separate table
**Computed columns**: Use GENERATED ALWAYS AS in SQL to store derived attributes that auto-update on change
**1:N for multi-valued**: Translate multi-valued attribute to separate table with FK back to parent entity
**When to store derived**: Only if computation is expensive and source data rarely changes, otherwise compute on demand

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: There are three main types of attributes in ER diagrams. A simple attribute is just a regular attribute that stores one atomic value. Like name or email. It shows up as a normal oval in the ER diagram and becomes a column in SQL. Straightforward. A derived attribute is calculated from other attributes, so you don't store it directly. Like age—you'd derive that from birth_date. In the ER diagram, derived attributes are shown with a dashed oval to indicate they're not physically stored. In SQL, you'd compute them in a view or use a generated column. For example, you could create a view that calculates age using the AGE function on birth_date. A multi-valued attribute can hold multiple values for one entity. The classic example is phone numbers—an employee might have a work phone, a mobile, and a home phone. In the ER diagram that's shown with a double oval. Here's where freshers mess up. You cannot store multi-valued attributes as a comma-separated string in one column. That breaks first normal form and makes querying impossible. The correct way is to create a separate table with a one-to-many relationship. So you'd have an employee_phone table with employee_id as a foreign key and one row per phone number. That way you can query, index, and enforce constraints properly. The key takeaway is each attribute type has a specific translation to SQL—simple becomes a column, derived becomes a computed view or generated column, and multi-valued becomes a separate table.

What is a composite attribute and how is it different from a multi-valued attribute?

Treat a multi-valued attribute like a simple one and you get comma-separated columns. That breaks first normal form. Store a derived value and it can drift out of date. The types steer you right.

Derived: a value you compute, like a post count from a query, usually not stored.
Multi-valued: many values like a post's tags, kept in a separate table.

Here's the non-obvious part. Store post count as a column and every new post must update it, or it goes stale.

questions.question: What is the difference between a weak entity and a strong entity?
questions.title: Weak Entity vs Strong Entity in ER Diagrams
questions.direct_answer: A strong entity has its own primary key and exists independently. A weak entity depends on a strong entity for its existence and identification—it does not have a complete primary key without the parent's key. Example: OrderItem is a weak entity dependent on Order.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of entity dependency and how it affects primary key design in relational schemas
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not recognizing that a weak entity requires the parent's primary key as part of its own primary key (composite key)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the double-rectangle notation in ER diagrams for weak entities and show a concrete SQL example with a composite primary key

sections.title: Strong vs Weak Entity Dependency
sections.content:
A **strong entity** can stand alone—it has a **primary key** made from its own attributes and doesn't depend on another entity for its identity. Customer, Product, Employee are strong entities: each has a customer_id, product_id, or emp_id that uniquely identifies it.

A **weak entity** cannot exist or be uniquely identified without a **parent strong entity**. It lacks a full primary key on its own and borrows part of its identity from the parent. In ER diagrams, weak entities are drawn with a **double rectangle** and connected to the parent with a **double diamond**. Example: OrderItem depends on Order. An item_number alone (like '1', '2', '3') isn't unique across all order items in the system—it's only unique within a specific order. So OrderItem has a **composite primary key** (order_id, item_number) where order_id is borrowed from the parent Order entity.

sections.title: Strong POST Owns Weak COMMENT (Identifying Relationship)
sections.content:
```mermaid
erDiagram
    POST ||--|{ COMMENT : owns
    POST {
        bigint post_id PK
        string title
    }
    COMMENT {
        bigint post_id PK "FK + part of key"
        int comment_num PK "partial key"
        string body
    }
```

POST is a strong entity with its own standalone key. COMMENT is weak: its identity is the parent's post_id plus a partial key comment_num. The solid identifying relationship shows COMMENT cannot exist or be identified without its owning POST.

sections.title: Strong Entity vs Weak Entity in DDL
sections.content:
```sql
-- Strong entity: has its own standalone primary key
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id     INT PRIMARY KEY,
    total  DECIMAL(10,2)
);

-- Weak entity: identified only together with its owner (order_id + line_no)
CREATE TABLE order_items (
    order_id INT,
    line_no  INT,                 -- partial key, unique only within an order
    product  VARCHAR(100),
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, line_no),          -- composite identity
    FOREIGN KEY (order_id) REFERENCES orders(id)
);
```

A weak entity borrows its owner's key to form a composite primary key and cannot exist without it.

sections.title: When to Model as Weak Entity
sections.content:
Use a weak entity when **identity is context-dependent**. Order line items are numbered 1, 2, 3 within each order, not globally unique. Hotel room numbers like '101' are unique within one hotel but repeated across hotels, so Room is weak relative to Hotel.

Use weak entities for **child records that have no meaning outside the parent context**—a Comment on a blog post is meaningless if the Post is deleted, so Comment is weak relative to Post. In Spring Boot with JPA, weak entities are modeled using **@Embeddable** composite keys or **@IdClass** with the parent's foreign key as part of the identifier, ensuring cascading deletes and referential integrity.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Giving weak entities independent primary keys**: Freshers add an auto-generated order_item_id to OrderItem, making it a strong entity and losing the semantic link to Order—now items can exist without an order, breaking business logic.
- **Not including parent FK in composite key**: Creating OrderItem with just item_number as the primary key, allowing duplicate item_numbers across different orders, violating uniqueness.
- **Weak entities without CASCADE delete**: When an Order is deleted but OrderItem rows remain orphaned because the FK lacks ON DELETE CASCADE, queries return inconsistent results and violate referential integrity constraints.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Strong entity**: Has its own complete primary key, exists independently, no dependency on other entities
**Weak entity**: Depends on a parent entity for existence and identity, requires composite primary key
**Composite primary key**: Combines parent's foreign key with weak entity's discriminator attribute (like item_number)
**ER notation**: Weak entities drawn with double rectangle, identifying relationship with double diamond
**Cascading deletes**: Weak entities must use ON DELETE CASCADE to maintain referential integrity when parent is deleted
**JPA modeling**: Use at-Embeddable composite key or at-IdClass with parent FK as part of the identifier
**Real-world examples**: OrderItem (depends on Order), Dependent (depends on Employee), Room (depends on Hotel)

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A strong entity has its own primary key and can exist independently. Think of a Customer table with customer_id—it doesn't need any other entity to identify itself. A weak entity depends on a strong entity for both its existence and its identity. The classic example is OrderItem. An order item doesn't make sense without an order, right? And the item number—like one, two, three—isn't unique across the whole database, only within a specific order. So OrderItem is weak and depends on Order. In the database, you'd use a composite primary key for the weak entity. For OrderItem that'd be order_id plus item_number. The order_id is a foreign key to the Order table, but it's also part of the primary key of OrderItem. In ER diagrams you show weak entities with a double rectangle and the relationship with a double diamond—that's called an identifying relationship. The practical impact is you must set up cascading deletes. If you delete an order, all its order items should be deleted automatically using ON DELETE CASCADE. Otherwise you get orphaned rows. In Spring Boot, you'd model this with an embedded composite key or use at-IdClass, and make sure your JPA relationship has cascade equals CascadeType dot ALL so deletions propagate correctly.

questions.question: How do you translate an ER diagram into a relational schema?
questions.title: Translating ER Diagram to SQL Tables
questions.direct_answer: Translation rules: Each entity becomes a table. Each attribute becomes a column. 1:N relationship—add FK to the N side. M:N—create a junction table with FKs to both entities. 1:1—add FK to either side (usually the optional side).

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to systematically convert an ER design into a normalized relational schema with correct foreign key placement
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing where to place the foreign key in a 1:N relationship (it always goes on the many side, not the one side)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through a complete multi-entity example showing entity-to-table, attribute-to-column, and all three cardinality types translated to SQL

sections.title: Systematic ER-to-SQL Translation
sections.content:
Translating an ER diagram into a relational schema follows a **mechanical set of rules** that freshers must memorize. Each **entity** becomes a **CREATE TABLE** statement.

Each **attribute** becomes a **column** with an appropriate data type (VARCHAR, INTEGER, DATE). The primary key attribute (underlined in the ER diagram) becomes a **PRIMARY KEY** constraint. **Relationships** are implemented with **foreign keys**, but the placement depends on cardinality. For **1:N**, the foreign key goes on the many side (N side) as a column referencing the one side's primary key. For **M:N**, you cannot use a single foreign key—you must create a **junction table** with foreign keys to both entities. For **1:1**, place the foreign key on whichever side is optional or dependent, and add a UNIQUE constraint to enforce one-to-one cardinality. This translation is not creative—it's a checklist you follow to produce a normalized schema that matches the ER design.

sections.title: The ER Diagram You Translate into Tables
Complete ER Diagram Translation Example
sections.content:
-- Entity: Customer (strong entity)
CREATE TABLE customer (
    customer_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,  -- Underlined attribute in ER
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE
);

-- Entity: Order (strong entity)
CREATE TABLE "order" (
    order_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    order_date DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE,
    customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL,        -- 1:N relationship, FK on N side
    CONSTRAINT fk_customer FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customer(customer_id)
);

-- Entity: Product (strong entity)
CREATE TABLE product (
    product_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    product_name VARCHAR(100),
    price DECIMAL(10,2)
);

-- M:N Relationship: Order contains many Products, Product in many Orders
CREATE TABLE order_item (               -- Junction table for M:N
    order_id BIGINT,
    product_id BIGINT,
    quantity INTEGER NOT NULL,          -- Relationship attribute
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id),
    CONSTRAINT fk_order FOREIGN KEY (order_id) REFERENCES "order"(order_id),
    CONSTRAINT fk_product FOREIGN KEY (product_id) REFERENCES product(product_id)
);

sections.title: When to Apply Translation Rules
sections.content:
Apply these rules in the **database design phase** after stakeholders approve the ER diagram but before writing application code.

Use them during **schema migrations** when adding new entities or relationships—draw the ER change first, translate to DDL, then run the migration.

Use them in **technical interviews** when asked to design a database schema on a whiteboard—sketch the ER diagram with entities and relationships, then verbally translate each piece to SQL: "Customer entity becomes a customer table, the one-to-many relationship to Order means order_id goes in the order table as a foreign key." In Spring Boot projects, translate the ER diagram to SQL DDL first, then map tables to JPA entities with the correct annotations (at-Entity, at-OneToMany, at-ManyToMany).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **FK on wrong side in 1:N**: Freshers put an order_id array or comma-separated list in the customer table instead of customer_id in the order table, inverting the relationship and breaking first normal form.
- **Translating M:N with single FK**: Attempting to implement a many-to-many relationship by adding a course_id column to student table, which only allows one course per student, not many.
- **Forgetting primary key constraints**: Creating tables without explicit PRIMARY KEY constraints, allowing duplicate or null identifiers that violate entity integrity.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Entity to table**: Each rectangle in ER diagram becomes a CREATE TABLE statement with entity name as table name
**Attribute to column**: Each oval becomes a column with data type matching attribute domain (string to VARCHAR, number to INTEGER)
**Primary key**: Underlined attribute in ER becomes PRIMARY KEY constraint in SQL
**1:N relationship**: Foreign key column added to the N side table, referencing the 1 side's primary key
**M:N relationship**: Cannot be directly implemented, requires junction table with two foreign keys and composite primary key
**1:1 relationship**: Foreign key on either side with UNIQUE constraint, prefer the optional or dependent entity
**Relationship attributes**: In M:N, attributes on the relationship diamond become columns in the junction table

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Translating an ER diagram to a relational schema is a step-by-step process. Each entity becomes a table. Each attribute becomes a column in that table. The underlined attribute—the primary key—gets a PRIMARY KEY constraint in SQL. Now for relationships, it depends on cardinality. For one-to-many, you add a foreign key to the many side. So if one customer has many orders, you put a customer_id foreign key column in the order table. For many-to-many, you can't use a single foreign key. You have to create a junction table with foreign keys to both entities. Like if students enroll in courses, you'd create an enrollment table with student_id and course_id, and a composite primary key of both columns. For one-to-one, you pick one side—usually the optional or dependent entity—and add a foreign key there with a UNIQUE constraint. Let me give you a full example. Say your ER diagram has Customer, Order, and Product. Customer to Order is one-to-many, so customer_id goes in the order table. Order to Product is many-to-many—one order has many products and one product appears in many orders. So you create an order_item junction table with order_id, product_id, and maybe a quantity column for relationship data. That's the systematic translation from abstract ER design to concrete SQL schema.

speakable_v2.standard_example: normalized MySQL schema for a blog app with users, posts, and comments
speakable_v2.hook: Turning an ER diagram into SQL is mechanical. Learn four rules and you've got it.

beats.text: Translating an ER diagram means turning each piece into SQL. Every entity becomes a table. Every attribute becomes a column. Every relationship becomes a foreign key or a junction table. There's a rule for each case.
Without fixed rules, people invent their own. They drop keys on the wrong side or skip junction tables. The result is a schema that breaks normal forms. The rules keep it clean.

items: Each entity becomes a table, and its key attribute becomes the primary key.
Each attribute becomes a column. A multi-valued one moves to its own table.
A one-to-many link adds a foreign key on the many side.
A many-to-many link gets a new junction table with two keys.

beats.text: Take our blog: User, Post, and Comment. A user writes many posts, so posts gets a user_id. A post has many comments, so comments gets a post_id. Posts and tags are many-to-many. Here's the non-obvious part. That last link can't be a column, so it needs a post_tags table.

items: Putting the foreign key on the one side. It always goes on the many side.
Forgetting relationship data, like a quantity that belongs in the junction table.

speakable_v2.cap: Four rules cover it: entity, attribute, one-to-many, and many-to-many. Apply them in order.
